description: Full ripple-tray apparatus comparing a wider aperture, nearly straight central crests and limited bending at their edges. Qualitative instantaneous crests, not an intensity/amplitude plot or a measured experiment.

ZH complete authoritative lesson: 波的衍射

在第47节讨论波的反射时，我们把反射面看作相对于波长很大的表面。
实际传播的波也会遇到与波长相近、甚至比波长更小的障碍物。
波长与障碍物大小的相对关系，决定了绕过障碍物的效应是否明显。

当露出水面的石头小于波长或与波长相近时，海浪可以绕过石头，在它后方继续传播，图96中的小石块就是这种情况。
把石头投入池塘激起的水波，也能绕过露出水面的树枝继续传播。
这些现象并不表示障碍物没有影响，而是说明波的传播不总能用直线路径来描述。

图96中的大石头说明了另一种情况：障碍物比波长大，尤其是远大于波长时，后方会形成振动较弱的区域，称为波影。
把波影看作完全没有波的区域，是一种近似；边缘绕行仍可能使较弱的波进入其中。

[fig-96]

图 96

声波也能传播到障碍物遮挡的区域，例如汽车还在房角后、看不见时，就可能先听到它的喇叭声。
在树林中，即使树干挡住了同伴的身影，呼喊声仍可能绕过树干传到同伴那里。
这里的绕行不等于声波必须穿透墙壁或树干。

声波和光波都能发生衍射，但可见光的波长比通常的声波波长小得多。
对于同样的房角或树干，声波的绕行效应往往更容易察觉，而光仍会形成明显的阴影。

**波在障碍物边缘或开口附近偏离直线传播、向其他方向展开的现象，称为衍射。**
衍射和干涉都是波动过程可能表现出的性质；水波、声波和光波都能发生衍射。

在水波的传播路径上放置带有窄缝的挡板，令缝宽小于波长，可以直观地观察衍射，如图97所示。
水波通过窄缝后向外展开，波面近似为圆弧，表现得像窄缝附近有一个振动的波源。
这与平直波面直接延续穿过开口的情形不同。

按照惠更斯原理，窄缝处彼此接近的次波源共同产生缝后的波。
当缝宽相对于波长及观察距离足够小时，可以近似把整个窄缝看作一个点波源；这不是说有限宽度的缝真的变成了一个点。

[fig-97]

图 97

[fig-98]

图 98

如果缝宽大于波长，尤其是远大于波长时，挡板后的波形会与窄缝情况不同，如图98所示。
开口中央的波面大致保持原来的平直形状，边缘附近的波面则发生弯曲。
这种边缘衍射使波能够部分进入挡板后方按直线传播本来不能到达的区域，而不是让整个宽缝都表现得像点波源。

惠更斯原理把已知波面上的各点看作次波源，有助于解释波为什么能够绕过障碍物边缘。
只用次波的几何包络来确定新波面，还不足以说明衍射图样的全部细节，例如不同位置的波强弱。

十九世纪初，法国学者菲涅耳进一步发展了这一解释。
**决定实际波场的不只是次波的包络，还包括各次波叠加时的干涉。**
将次波的振幅和相位一并考虑，才能更完整地描述衍射，这就是惠更斯与菲涅耳观点之间的重要联系。

EN complete authoritative lesson: Diffraction of Waves

In Section 47, the reflecting surface was treated as large compared with the wavelength.
In practice, a traveling wave may also meet an obstacle comparable to its wavelength, or even smaller.
The relative sizes of the wavelength and the obstacle help determine how noticeable the bending of the wave will be.

When a stone sticking out of the water is smaller than the wavelength, or comparable to it, water waves can bend around it and continue behind it, as with the small stone in Figure 96.
Waves made by dropping a stone into a pond can similarly pass around branches sticking out of the water.
The obstacle still affects the wave, but straight paths alone do not describe its propagation.

The large stone in Figure 96 illustrates a different case: an obstacle larger than the wavelength, especially much larger, can leave a region of weaker wave motion behind it, called a wave shadow.
Treating that region as completely wave-free is an approximation; diffraction around the edges can still carry weaker waves into it.

[fig-96]

Figure 96

Sound can reach places hidden behind an obstacle: you may hear a car's horn before you can see the car around a building corner.
In a wooded area, a call may reach a companion whose view is blocked by a tree trunk.
Bending around an obstacle does not mean that the sound must pass through the wall or the trunk.

Both sound and light diffract, but visible light has a much shorter wavelength than ordinary sound.
For the same building corner or tree trunk, the bending of sound is often more noticeable, while light still produces a clear shadow.

**Diffraction is the spreading of waves away from straight-line propagation near an obstacle's edge or an opening.**
Like interference, diffraction is a property that wave processes can exhibit; water waves, sound, and light can all diffract.

Place a barrier with a slit narrower than the wavelength in the path of water waves to observe diffraction, as in Figure 97.
Beyond the narrow slit, the wavefronts spread out as approximately circular arcs, as though a vibrating source were near the opening.
They do not simply continue as the incoming straight wavefronts.

In Huygens' principle, closely spaced secondary wave sources at the slit combine to produce the waves beyond it.
When the slit is sufficiently small compared with the wavelength and the observation distance, it can be approximated as a point source; a slit of finite width does not literally become a point.

[fig-97]

Figure 97

[fig-98]

Figure 98

When the slit is wider than the wavelength, especially much wider, the waves beyond the barrier differ from the narrow-slit case, as in Figure 98.
The central parts of the wavefronts remain nearly straight, while the wavefronts bend near the edges.
This edge diffraction lets waves partly enter the region behind the barrier that straight paths would not reach; the whole wide opening does not behave like a point source.

Huygens' principle treats points on a known wavefront as secondary wave sources, helping explain why waves can bend around an obstacle's edge.
The geometrical envelope of those secondary waves alone does not explain every detail of a diffraction pattern, such as the strengths of the waves at different positions.

In the early nineteenth century, the French scientist Fresnel developed this explanation further.
**The actual wave field depends not just on an envelope, but also on interference as the secondary waves superpose.**
Including both their amplitudes and their phases gives a fuller account of diffraction, connecting the ideas of Huygens and Fresnel.

inventory.description: One low oblique quadrilateral tray, with outlined rear/side rims, long front wall and dark foot/support details below the front.
One bounded water surface with incident and transmitted regions; same affine projection as the tray.
Repeated incident approximately parallel crests. Five strokes are a declared modern sampling choice, not a source numerical count.

Successive right-side fronts remain mainly straight/parallel and occupy the region aligned with the opening; they do not become the fully fanning arc family of figure97. Front ends show limited edge curvature.
Two aligned screen portions with exactly one interruption/opening. Faces and cap edges are one screen, not extra screens.
One large aperture between the screen ends opens the left wave region to the right; no dimension, scale or printed ratio is provided.
One near-horizontal rod enters from the left across the tray rim to the drive paddle.
One prominent paddle-like source stroke at the entering rod end, with no added motor or labels.
Same tray/source apparatus as fig97, with a wider single aperture; numerical widths exist only in the author's nondimensional geometry model.
The transmitted centres remain straight and parallel to the incident crests, rather than becoming point-source arcs.
Only the ends of each wide-slit front bend into regions beyond straight continuation of the opening.
